newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda president tells Kabila to wait before polls.
newsitem.headline: Uganda president tells Kabila to wait before polls.

text.p: Uganda's president on Wednesday advised Laurent Kabila, self-proclaimed president of the new Democratic Republic of Congo, to wait up to three years before elections.

President Yoweri Museveni, a former rebel leader himself and widely seen as Kabila's mentor, declined to comment on whether Uganda was involved in supporting the rebellion which ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko, saying that he had secrets to keep.

"My advice to Mr Kabila would be to unite Zaire now. The first job would be to maintain this unity by forming a broad-based government," he told a news conference on his return from a visit to London.
He warned Kabila not to include too many politicians from other groups at the expense of his own people. "He (Kabila) must not lose control. His own supporters should be the majority," Museveni said.

Museveni said the next step for Kabila should be to develop his country's poor infrastructure, especially roads, and stabilise the economy, something which he said he had already discussed with the new president.
Museveni, who since seizing power in 1986 after a five-year bush war has barred political parties from contesting elections, cautioned Kabila against bowing to pressure from the West for quick polls.

"If he (Kabila) forms a broad-based government which is inclusive, they could wait for some time -- two to three years," said the Ugandan president, who rules through his former rebel National Resistance Movement.
Museveni made his comments as Kabila prepared in Kinshasa to name his government and was under Western pressure to make it broad-based and a first step towards multi-party elections.

Asked about Ugandan involvement in the rebellion, Museveni said: "When people are fighting a war like the one in Zaire they have secrets and since I am not one who gives information on secrets I won't tell you."

Western intelligence sources have said Ugandan and Rwandan forces fought alongside Kabila's rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo in the rebellion that began in the east last October.
Accused by Mobutu of intervening, Uganda and Rwanda denied direct involvement but have expressed support for the rebellion.
Museveni said he considered Zaire and other countries in the Great Lakes region of Central Africa as part of Uganda's local, not foreign, policy as only colonial boundaries separated them.
"These are our people," the Ugandan president added.
He hit out at U.N. protests at the alliance's treatment of Hutu Rwandan refugees and accusations it was following a policy of extermination by blocking aid agency access and killing them.
"If I was to award marks for mistreating refugees, I think 70 percent would go to the U.N.," said Museveni, adding Alliance forces were too young and ill-equipped for mass extermination.
Museveni said he had lent his presidential jet to Kabila several times because he regarded him as a freedom fighter.

"I was giving this plane to Kabila because I wanted to get peace. Our plane is the one which took him to Rwanda," said Museveni, adding that once U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun asked him to lend his jet to the rebel leader, who proclaimed himself president of the Democratic Republic of the Congo on Saturday.
